transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

Not necessarily. A heat-pump dryer runs much cooler and is normally substantially slower than an old condenser dryer, so feeling only mildly warm early on is expected; towels can take a few hours, particularly on an Eco setting or with a heavy load. Nearly 3½ hours can still be plausible, but it is worth ruling out restricted airflow first, as that makes them much slower. With the dryer switched off, clean the door fluff filter and, if yours has one behind a lower flap, the second filter as the instructions specify; also empty the water container. Was this a normal Cotton/Towels programme rather than Eco, Delicates or low heat, and are both filters clean? If towels are still properly wet at the end of a full cycle after that, it would be less normal and may need an engineer to assess the heat-pump system or sensors.

Yes it's the Cotton Cupboard Dry programme with the load full, not Eco. I clean the fluff filters after every load and the other filter two weeks ago, looks clean. The water container fills up with loads of water each cycle too. Towels do come out fully dry in the end, it just takes forever!

It does not currently sound like a clear fault. The tank filling and the towels ending fully dry show it is removing moisture; a heat-pump dryer is meant to feel only moderately warm and a full towel load can genuinely take around this long on Cotton Cupboard Dry. The most useful comparison is the washing-machine spin and load size: towels hold a huge amount of water, and a full drum gives the air less room to circulate. Try a load no more than two-thirds full, washed at the highest spin suitable for towels (usually 1,200–1,400 rpm). If that drops the time substantially, the dryer is behaving normally. If a smaller, well-spun load still takes 3½ hours or more, despite the filters being clean, the remaining possibilities are a restricted internal air path or an underperforming heat-pump system, which would need an engineer rather than a heater-element repair.
My washer only spins at 1000 rpm, so I can't really go higher than that. Is it normal for it to take this long though? Could it be because it's in my garage, which is about 8-10 C at the moment?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Yes — an 8–10°C garage can absolutely make a heat-pump dryer slower. It relies on a refrigeration system to recover heat, and cold surrounding air makes that process less efficient; combined with a full load of heavy towels spun at 1,000 rpm, around 3½ hours can be normal rather than a fault. The best way to separate normal performance from a fault is one test with the drum only about two-thirds full. If that cuts the drying time noticeably, the dryer is behaving as expected in those conditions. If a reduced, 1,000-rpm towel load still takes about 3½ hours or longer with clean filters, an engineer should check the internal airflow path and heat-pump performance.
Ok so the garage being cold could explain it then? I can't really move it indoors though. I do open the door two or three times during a cycle to check on it, does that make any difference?

Yes, the cold garage could explain a significant part of it. At 8–10°C a heat-pump dryer has less heat available to recover, and full towels coming from a 1,000 rpm spin contain a lot of water; it can therefore take far longer than the old hotter condenser dryer while still drying properly. Opening the door two or three times will add some time, because it lets the warm air out and the dryer may pause and re-assess the load when restarted. It should not by itself turn a normal cycle into a 3½-hour one, but it makes judging the early warmth less useful—try leaving it shut for the first hour if you can. The best deciding test is a two-thirds-full towel load on the same programme. If that finishes noticeably sooner, this points to normal performance for the installation and laundry conditions. If it still takes around 3½ hours or more, despite clean filters, an engineer should assess internal airflow and the sealed heat-pump system.
